# Technical Specification: Single-Pass Inkjet Recording Method for Low-Thermal-Conductivity Substrates

## 1. Field of Invention and Overview
The present invention relates to an advanced single-pass inkjet recording method designed to print high-resolution, high-quality color images on challenging substrates. Specifically, the method overcomes the thermal dissipation issues typically associated with printing on thick media characterized by low thermal conductivity. By utilizing a specially formulated set of active ray-curing inks with precisely controlled gelation temperatures, this process prevents color bleeding and ink pooling during high-speed, single-pass operation.

## 2. Substrate Specifications
The recording method is optimized for demanding substrates that present heat-retention and absorption challenges. To achieve the benefits of this invention, the targeted recording medium must satisfy the following physical constraints:
* **Thickness:** The medium must have a total thickness of **at least 0.4 mm**.
* **Thermal Conductivity:** The medium must exhibit a thermal conductivity of **less than 0.10 W/(m·K)**.

These parameters typically characterize heavy-duty packaging materials, rigid plastics, or specialized insulated boards, which tend to retain localized heat and disrupt standard ink-curing dynamics.

## 3. Ink Set Composition and Gelation Dynamics
The printing process employs an ink set containing **at least two active ray-curing color inks** (such as UV-curable or electron beam-curable inks). The core innovation of this method relies on a strictly controlled gelation temperature gradient among the inks, arranged according to the media conveyance direction (from upstream to downstream):

* **Upstream to Downstream Temperature Differential:** In any applicable ink configuration, the color ink positioned at the most downstream location must have a gelation temperature that is **3.0°C to 15.0°C higher** than that of the ink positioned at the most upstream location.
* **Progressive Gelation Profile (3+ Inks):** When the system utilizes an ink set consisting of three or more colors, the gelation temperatures must follow a non-decreasing profile along the print path. Specifically, each subsequent ink applied along the conveyance direction must possess a gelation temperature that is **equal to or higher than** the gelation temperature of the immediately adjacent upstream ink.

## 4. Technical Advantage and Mechanism
By enforcing this progressive gelation temperature hierarchy ($T_{\text{upstream}} \le \dots \le T_{\text{downstream}}$), the liquid stability and pinning rates of newly applied ink droplets are optimized as the substrate moves through the printing line. 

On thick, low-thermal-conductivity media, previously deposited inks retain thermal energy differently than the cool substrate. Matching and progressively increasing the gelation temperatures of downstream inks prevents unwanted spreading, color mixing (bleed), and phase-change instability. As a result, this single-pass inkjet method ensures crisp dot retention, seamless multi-color overlay, and superior final image quality at industrial production speeds.

# Single-Pass Inkjet Recording Method and Ink Set for Low-Thermal-Conductance Substrates

## 1. Field of the Invention and Background
Inkjet recording technology has expanded rapidly from traditional paper-based printing to industrial applications involving a wide variety of rigid and thick substrates, including plastics, composite panels, and heavy packaging materials. In high-speed industrial printing, **single-pass inkjet recording systems**—where the recording medium travels under a stationary series of printheads—are preferred due to their immense throughput capacity.

However, printing high-resolution color images onto thick substrates with poor thermal conductivity presents severe technical challenges. When an active ray-curing ink (such as a UV-curable ink) is jetted onto a substrate that acts as a thermal insulator, heat management on the medium’s surface becomes unpredictable. The combination of localized heat from printhead elements, ambient curing lamps, and friction can cause surface temperatures to rise incrementally as the substrate passes under successive printheads. 

On low-thermal-conductance media, this trapped heat lowers the viscosity of newly deposited ink droplets, causing uncontrolled ink spreading, poor dot placement, inter-color bleeding (color mixing), and severe image degradation.

---

## 2. Technical Solution Overview
To overcome these thermal limitations without sacrificing printing speed or image resolution, a novel single-pass inkjet recording method utilizes a specialized active ray-curing gel ink set tailored for insulating media. 

This system relies on precise control of the physical phase-change properties—specifically the **gelation temperature ($T_g$)**—of the inks across the printing line. By establishing a progressive thermal gradient within the ink set, the method guarantees that ink droplets solidify predictably upon contact, regardless of the thermal energy accumulated by the substrate during transit.

---

## 3. Substrate Specifications
The method is specifically engineered for challenging media that meet the following physical criteria:
*   **Thickness:** Equal to or greater than **0.4 mm**.
*   **Thermal Conductivity:** Less than **0.10 W/(m·K)**.

Representative examples of such media include foamed polyolefin sheets, thick PVC boards, corrugated plastic panels, and specialized insulated packaging materials. Due to their low thermal conductivity, these materials cannot efficiently dissipate heat downward through their bulk, forcing heat to accumulate on the top printing surface.

---

## 4. Ink Set Architecture and Thermal Gradient Control
The ink set comprises multiple color channels (e.g., Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Black, and optional spot colors) arranged sequentially along the direction of substrate transport. The inks are **active ray-curing phase-change inks** (gel inks) that exist in a fluid, low-viscosity liquid state when heated inside the printhead, but rapidly transition into a high-viscosity gel state as they cool upon impacting the medium.

To counter the rising surface temperature of the substrate as it moves downstream, the ink set is formulated according to two critical rules:

1.  **Monotonic Gelation Profile:** Any given ink positioned downstream along the transport line must have a gelation temperature ($T_g$) equal to or higher than the inks positioned upstream from it:
    $$T_{g, \text{downstream}} \ge T_{g, \text{upstream}}$$

2.  **Differential Temperature Range:** The gelation temperature of the ink in the **most downstream position** must be **3.0°C to 15.0°C higher** than that of the ink in the **most upstream position**:
    $$\Delta T_g = T_{g, \text{most downstream}} - T_{g, \text{most upstream}} = 3.0^\circ\text{C} \text{ to } 15.0^\circ\text{C}$$

### *Mechanistic Rationale for the Temperature Range:*
*   **If $\Delta T_g < 3.0^\circ\text{C}$:** The thermal gradient is insufficient. Downstream ink droplets will encounter a pre-warmed substrate surface, slowing their cooling rate. This prevents immediate gelation, leading to ink bleeding into previously deposited upstream layers.
*   **If $\Delta T_g > 15.0^\circ\text{C}$:** The gelation temperature of the final downstream ink becomes excessively high, requiring unrealistically high printhead jetting temperatures. This risks thermal degradation of the ink components and leads to instability during jetting.

---

## 5. Printing Process and Operational Mechanism

```
Substrate Travel Direction --->
[ Upstream Printhead ]  --->  [ Midstream Printhead ]  --->  [ Downstream Printhead ]  ---> [ UV Lamp ]
(Lower Ink Tg)                (Medium Ink Tg)               (Highest Ink Tg)                (Final Cure)
Substrate: Cool               Substrate: Warming            Substrate: Warmest
```

1.  **Upstream Injection:** The substrate enters the machine at ambient temperature. The most upstream printhead jets ink with the lowest $T_g$. Upon contacting the relatively cool substrate, the ink drops cool rapidly below their $T_g$ and form stable, localized gels.
2.  **Heat Accumulation:** As the substrate advances, it absorbs radiant heat from ambient equipment and pinning lights, causing its surface temperature to rise.
3.  **Downstream Injection:** When the warmer substrate reaches downstream printheads, it encounters inks formulated with progressively higher $T_g$ values. Because the gelation threshold of these downstream inks is higher, they undergo phase change at higher surface temperatures, achieving instantaneous gelation despite the pre-heated medium.
4.  **Final Fixation:** Once all ink layers are pinned in their gel states, the substrate passes under a primary active-ray curing lamp (e.g., UV-LED), cross-linking the polymer matrix to form a durable, high-gloss image.

---

## 6. Conclusion and Benefits
By matching the thermodynamic behavior of the ink set to the heat dissipation characteristics of low-conductance materials, this method eliminates the trade-offs traditionally associated with printing on thick, insulating media. 

**Key Benefits Include:**
*   **Prevention of Inter-Color Bleeding:** Drops gel instantly upon contact, preventing neighboring colors from mixing.
*   **Superior Pinpoint Accuracy:** Suppresses satellite drops and droplet migration.
*   **High Processing Speed:** Fully compatible with high-speed single-pass manufacturing lines without requiring external substrate cooling equipment.

Based on the technical parameters of such an invention, here is a structured summary of the key claims typically found in a patent application for a **single-pass active ray-curing inkjet method that regulates ink gelation temperatures on low-thermal-conductance substrates**.

---

### **1. Primary Independent Method Claim (Core Process)**
The application claims a method for single-pass inkjet printing comprising the following sequential steps performed during a single relative movement between a printing system and a low-thermal-conductance substrate:
*   **Ink Jetting:** Ejecting a hot-melt, temperature-sensitive gel ink (heated above its sol-gel transition temperature, $T_{sol}$) from an inkjet head onto the substrate.
*   **Thermal Regulation:** Regulating the surface temperature of the substrate to maintain it within a specific gelation temperature window ($T_{gel} \le T_{substrate} < T_{sol}$) immediately before, during, or immediately after ink impact.
*   **Droplet Pinning:** Allowing the ink droplets to undergo a liquid-to-gel phase transition, locking the droplet diameter (dot gain) on the low-thermal-conductance surface.
*   **Active Ray Curing:** Irradiating the gelled ink droplets with active energy rays (e.g., UV-LED or electron beam) in the same pass to crosslink and fully cure the ink resin.

---

### **2. Temperature Regulation & Thermal Management Claims**
Because low-thermal-conductance substrates (e.g., thin plastic films, flexible packaging, paper) dissipate heat poorly, heat from both the hot ink and the active ray curing unit can cause substrate deformation or prevent proper gelation. The patent claims specific thermal control mechanisms:

*   **Active Underside Cooling/Heating:** Claims a thermal control platen or drum directly beneath the substrate that actively adds or removes heat to compensate for the low thermal conductivity of the material.
*   **Exothermic Compensation:** Claims a dynamic feedback loop that measures the cumulative heat imparted by the UV/LED curing lamp and adjusts the substrate platen temperature downstream to prevent the gelled ink from re-melting ($T_{substrate}$ rising back to $T_{sol}$).
*   **Pre-Conditioning Zone:** Claims a pre-heating or pre-cooling zone upstream of the printhead that sets the low-thermal-conductance substrate to a uniform baseline temperature prior to ink ejection.

---

### **3. Material Parameter & Property Claims**
*   **Substrate Specification:** Claims the method specifically for substrates having a thermal conductivity below a defined threshold (typically $< 0.5 \text{ W/m}\cdot\text{K}$, such as PET, PP, PE, or thin film foils).
*   **Ink Phase-Change Profile:** Claims the use of radiation-curable ink containing a gelling agent (e.g., wax-based or amide-based gelling agents) characterized by a sharp viscosity change within a narrow temperature window (e.g., between $40^\circ\text{C}$ and $70^\circ\text{C}$).

---

### **4. Apparatus Configuration Claims (System Layout)**
The patent claims a physical printing apparatus arranged for high-speed single-pass execution, including:
*   **Sequential Spatial Layout:** A printhead module, a thermal regulation module, and an active-ray irradiation unit arranged sequentially along a continuous substrate conveyance path.
*   **Distance/Time Delay Claims:** Specific spatial distances between the jetting zone and the curing zone, ensuring the ink remains in the gel state for a precise duration (e.g., milliseconds) to allow controlled levelling without line bleeding before exposure to active rays.

---

### **5. Process Control & Quality Claims**
*   **Controlled Dot Gain:** Claims the ability to achieve a target dot diameter and ink film thickness independent of printing speed by holding the substrate within the tight $T_{gel}$ boundary.
*   **Prevention of Thermal Distortion:** Claims a method that prevents thermal shrinking, wrinkling, or stretching of heat-sensitive, low-conductance films by limiting the maximum substrate temperature during the single pass.

---

### **Summary of Novelty / Main Technical Advantage**
The primary inventive step claimed is the **active management of the substrate's local thermal boundary layer**. By overcoming the natural heat-retention limitation of low-conductance substrates, the method enables high-speed single-pass printing of UV-gel inks with precise image quality (no bleed or feathering) and zero substrate damage.

To achieve **high-quality color inkjet printing** on media that is both **thick ($\ge 0.4\text{ mm}$)** and has **low thermal conductivity ($< 0.10\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$)**—such as foamed PVC, expanded polystyrene, cork, heavy paperboard, or synthetic insulation sheets—you must carefully match the **ink technology** and **media feed mechanism** to these physical properties.

Here is a technical guide and recommended printer options tailored to your criteria.

---

### 1. Key Technical Constraints & Solutions

*   **Thermal Conductivity Problem ($< 0.10\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$):** 
    *   *Why it matters:* Technologies like **Latex** or **Eco-Solvent** rely heavily on high-temperature heating zones (60°C to 110°C) to cure or dry the ink. Because your media dissipates heat very poorly, surface heat builds up rapidly, leading to **thermal distortion, media buckling, or uneven ink drying**.
    *   *Solution:* Use **UV-LED Curable Inkjet** technology. UV-LED systems use cold-curing light (very low heat transfer) to instantly polymerize ink on the substrate surface without relying on thermal absorption.
*   **Media Thickness ($\ge 0.4\text{ mm}$ / ~400+ microns):**
    *   *Why it matters:* Standard desktop printers bend media around rollers, which damages thick, rigid, or semi-rigid substrates.
    *   *Solution:* You need a printer with a **flatbed architecture** or a **straight-through media path** with an adjustable printhead clearance (platen height adjustment).

---

### 2. Recommended Printer Technologies & Models

#### **Option A: UV-LED Flatbed Inkjet (Best Overall for Synthetics, Foam, & Rigid Media)**
*Ideal if the material is non-porous (e.g., foamed PVC, acrylic, leather, cork) and requires high durability and color vibrancy.*

*   **Why it fits:** Cold UV-LED curing generates virtually no thermal stress. The media stays flat on a rigid bed (often vacuum-assisted), and printhead height can be adjusted from 0.5 mm up to 100+ mm.
*   **Recommended Models:**
    1.  **Roland VersaSTUDIO BD-8 (Desktop UV Flatbed):**
        *   *Max Thickness:* Up to 102 mm (4 inches).
        *   *Print Quality:* High-resolution ECO-UV 5 inks (CMYK + White + Gloss/Primer).
        *   *Best for:* Small-to-medium prints on thick, low-conductivity objects and sheets.
    2.  **Mimaki UJF-3042 MkII e / UJF-6042 MkII e:**
        *   *Max Thickness:* Up to 153 mm.
        *   *Print Resolution:* Up to 1200 $\times$ 1200 dpi (Photorealistic fine art quality).
        *   *Best for:* High-precision industrial and commercial color printing with variable dot technology.
    3.  **Mutoh ValueJet 426UF / 626UF:**
        *   *Max Thickness:* Up to 70 mm (426) or 150 mm (626).
        *   *Best for:* Prototyping and short-run production on heat-sensitive thick substrates.

---

#### **Option B: Fine Art / Professional Photo Aqueous Inkjet (Best for Coated Paperboards)**
*Ideal ONLY IF the media is porous/coated for aqueous ink (e.g., heavy cotton rag, museum board, thick cardboard).*

*   **Why it fits:** Pigment-based aqueous inks do not require intense heat to dry (drying occurs via absorption and ambient evaporation).
*   **Recommended Models:**
    1.  **Epson SureColor P900 (17-inch Desktop):**
        *   *Max Thickness:* Up to **1.5 mm** via the dedicated Fine Art / Poster Board straight-through path.
        *   *Print Quality:* Exceptional (UltraChrome PRO10 ink system, 10-color).
        *   *Note:* Thermal conductivity is not an issue since ambient drying is used, but the media **must** have an inkjet-receptive coating.
    2.  **Epson SureColor P7570 / P9570 (24" / 44" Wide Format):**
        *   *Max Thickness:* Up to **1.5 mm** (straight top-loading feeder).
        *   *Print Quality:* Commercial photo grade (12-color ink system).
    3.  **Canon imagePROGRAF PRO-1000:**
        *   *Max Thickness:* Up to **0.7 mm** via manual feed slot.

---

### 3. Summary Comparison for Selection

| Criteria | **UV-LED Flatbed Printers** (e.g., Mimaki UJF, Roland BD-8) | **Aqueous Photo Printers** (e.g., Epson SC-P900) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Compatible Materials** | Virtually any surface (Plastics, Foam, Wood, Metal, Paperboard) | **Must be coated for aqueous inkjet** (Paper, Canvas) |
| **Thermal Sensitivity Handling** | **Excellent** (Cold LED light, zero thermal warping) | **Good** (Ambient drying, no heaters required) |
| **Max Thickness Range** | 0.1 mm to **100+ mm** | Up to **1.5 mm** |
| **Color Quality** | High (CMYK + Spot White + Clear/Varnish) | Superior (9–12 Ink Pigment Systems for photo color management) |
| **Ink Drying Method** | Instant UV Polymerization | Evaporation / Absorption |

---

### 4. Recommendation Checklist

1. **If your material is non-porous (Plastic, Foam, Cork, Rubber):** 
   $\rightarrow$ Choose a **UV-LED Flatbed printer** (e.g., *Roland BD-8* for compact spaces, or *Mimaki UJF series* for higher speed/precision).

2. **If your material is a thick fiber/paperboard ($\le 1.5\text{ mm}$):** 
   $\rightarrow$ Choose a **Straight-path Aqueous Pigment printer** (e.g., *Epson SureColor P900* or *P7570*). 

3. **Avoid:** 
   * **Latex Printers** (e.g., HP Latex series) – High heat curing will melt or warp low-conductivity substrates.
   * **Standard Roll-to-Roll Inkjets** – Rigid 0.4mm+ media will jam or crack on curved paper paths.

The entire image or functional layer across the full width of the substrate is deposited in a **single pass**, achieving extremely high linear production speeds. * **Active Ray-Curing Inks:** Liquids composed of monomers, oligomers, photoinitiators, and pigments/additives that polymerize (instantly solidify) when exposed to electromagnetic radiation (typically **UV-LED**, **UV-Mercury**, or **Electron Beam [EB]**). * **2+ Inks:** A multi-channel system utilizing two or more distinct inks. These can be process colors (e.g., CMYK), specialized coatings (white, varnish, primer), or functional materials (conductive, insulating, dielectric inks). --- ### **2. Process Architecture & Workflow** In a multi-ink single-pass system, the spatial arrangement of the printheads and radiation sources is critical to prevent ink bleeding and ensure layer integrity. ```text [ Substrate Motion: Direction of Travel ---> ] ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | Station 1 | Pin-Cure 1 | Station 2 | Pin-Cure 2 | ... | Final Full-Cure | | (Ink A / White)| (Low UV) | (Ink B / CMYK)| (Low UV) | | (High-Intensity UV/EB)| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ``` #### **Step-by-Step Mechanism:** 1. **Substrate Transport:** Precision web/conveyor handling maintains ultra-stable linear motion (speeds ranging from $30 \text{ m/min}$ to $300+ \text{ m/min}$). 2. **First Ink Deposition (Ink 1):** High-frequency piezoelectric drop-on-demand (DoD) printheads eject droplets of Ink 1. 3. **Inter-Station Pin-Curing (Intermediate Curing):** * A low-intensity radiation source (usually UV-LED) partially cures (gelates) Ink 1. * **Purpose:** Increases ink viscosity, freezes the dot boundary (controlling drop gain), and prevents mixing (bleed) with subsequent inks without fully hardening the surface. 4. **Subsequent Ink Deposition (Inks 2 to N):** Sequential deposition of additional colors, primers, or functional materials onto the pinned surface. 5. **Final Full-Cure (Cross-Linking):** * A high-intensity radiation lamp (UV-LED, Medium-Pressure Mercury Vapor, or Electron Beam) floods the substrate. * **Result:** Triggers complete polymerization/cross-linking across all deposited ink layers, forming a durable, fully solid matrix bonded to the substrate. --- ### **3. Chemical & Physical Dynamics** #### **A. Ray-Curing Chemistry (UV vs. EB)** * **Free-Radical UV Curing:** UV photon breaks down photoinitiators $\rightarrow$ generates free radicals $\rightarrow$ initiates rapid chain-growth polymerization of acrylate monomers/oligomers. * **Cationic UV Curing:** Used for specific substrates requiring low shrinkage and high adhesion; less inhibited by atmospheric oxygen. * **Electron Beam (EB) Curing:** High-energy electrons directly break chemical bonds to form radicals without photoinitiators (ideal for food-safe packaging to eliminate photoinitiator migration). #### **B. Rheology & Wetting** * **Viscosity:** UV inks generally require low dynamic viscosity at jetting temperature ($8 - 15 \text{ cP}$ at $40–50^\circ\text{C}$). * **Surface Tension Gradient:** To achieve optimal trapping (stacking of Ink 2 on Ink 1), the surface tension of Ink 2 must be lower than the surface energy of the pinned Ink 1. --- ### **4. Key Advantages** 1. **Extreme Throughput:** Speeds up to $100–300 \text{ m/min}$ make it competitive with analog flexographic or gravure printing while retaining digital variability. 2. **Substrate Versatility:** Because inks cure instantly on the surface, the process works on non-porous materials (plastics, glass, metals, coated paperboard) without thermal distortion. 3. **Zero VOC Emissions:** Active ray-curable inks are typically $100\%$ solids (solvent-free), drastically reducing volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions. 4. **High Durability:** Ray-cured polymers exhibit superior chemical, solvent, scratch, and heat resistance. 5. **Multi-Layer Stacking:** Enables tactile printing (embossing effects), functional layering (3D structure/printed electronics), and high-opacity white undercoats in a single inline process. --- ### **5. Engineering Challenges & Solutions** | Challenge | Cause | Technical Mitigation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Nozzle Clogging via Stray Light** | Reflection of UV/Ray energy back into the printhead nozzle faceplate initiates curing inside nozzles. | • Light shields/baffling between cure units and printhead faces.
• Recirculating printhead architectures (keep ink moving). | | **Oxygen Inhibition** | Atmospheric $O_2$ quenches free radicals, leaving a tacky/uncured surface on thin ink films. | • Nitrogen purging ($\text{N}_2$ inerting environment).
• High peak-irradiance UV-LEDs ($395\text{nm}$ / $365\text{nm}$). | | **Inter-Layer Adhesion Defect** | Over-pinning Ink 1 creates a fully cured surface, preventing Ink 2 from chemically bonding to it. | • Precise dose control (mJ/cm²) of inter-station pin-curing lamps. | | **Nozzle-Out Banding** | In single-pass systems, a single clogged nozzle creates a visible line along the entire web length. | • High-frequency active nozzle redundancy/stitching.
• Inline vision systems with real-time drop compensation. | --- ### **6. Primary Industrial Applications** 1. **Digital Label & Packaging Printing:** High-speed CMYK + High-Opacity White printing on flexible film (PE, PET, OPP) and corrugated boards. 2. **Industrial Decor & Surfaces:** Direct-to-shape printing on laminate flooring, ceramics, glass, and edge-banding. 3. **Printed Electronics & Functional Additive:** Depositing layers of conductive metallic ink, insulating UV dielectric resins, and structural materials sequentially. 4. **Additive Manufacturing (Inkjet-based 3D Printing):** Material Jetting processes (e.g., Stratasys PolyJet) jetting multiple photopolymer formulations per pass to create multi-material solid parts.
